items.title: Nvidia Q3 FY27 under interim CEO Colette Kress — record $115.8B revenue (+103% YoY), $107.6B data center, Vera Rubin NVL72 shipping, Q4 guided to $130B ±3% with zero China compute; board chair Harvey Jones says the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
items.summary: Nvidia reported Q3 fiscal 2027 on Tuesday, November 17, 2026 — the first earnings call in 33 years not led by Jensen Huang, after his November 11 resignation. Headline results beat Wall Street expectations across the board. Total revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year and 20% sequentially (consensus ~$109.1 billion per LSEG/CNBC). Data center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110% YoY (vs ~$101.9 billion Street estimate) and ~93% of the total. Non-GAAP EPS was $2.68 against $2.47 expected; GAAP EPS was $2.70. The 'edge computing' bucket (gaming, PCs, automotive, robotics) was $8.2 billion, +42% YoY. Kress said Vera Rubin NVL72 racks began shipping in the quarter, with purchase orders from every major hyperscaler, AI cloud, and system OEM — Nvidia calls it the fastest product ramp in company history. Q4 guidance was $130 billion in revenue ±3% against ~$124.9 billion consensus, with a 71–72% gross margin outlook; the quarter contains an extra week, and the forecast explicitly assumes zero data center compute revenue from China. Stock rose roughly 2–2.5% after-hours. The leadership thread hardened the same afternoon: board chair Harvey C. Jones told reporters on November 17 that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang — directly addressing public calls from Elon Musk and endorsements from President Donald Trump, and a comment from Huang himself that he would return if the board invited him back. Huang is scheduled to appear before congressional committees on December 1, with Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter scheduled for December 2, as part of a national-security inquiry linked to reporting that one of the relationships cited in his departure involved a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a Beijing intelligence asset. The permanent-CEO search continues; press speculation still centers on AMD's Lisa Su, Arm's Rene Haas (a former Nvidia executive), Apple CEO Tim Cook (Trump-endorsed), Intel's Lip-Bu Tan, and Kress as an internal candidate — no board shortlist has been confirmed. Nvidia primary domains (nvidia.com, investor.nvidia.com) remain DNS-blocked from this egress; actuals above are corroborated across CNBC, stockanalysis.com, Newsquawk, TechPowerUp, TradingKey, Credence Research, Panabee, Cellcog, BBN Times, Vested Finance, Constellation Research, 247WallSt, Pepperstone, Barchart, Stocktwits, Decrypt, Crypto Briefing, oninvest, Yahoo Finance, IBTimes, FXStreet, and Asianetnews.
items.why_it_matters: Overnight enrichment settled three of the four 30-day watch questions from yesterday's pm digest in a single afternoon. First, the $108B consensus-vs-print test: Nvidia didn't just clear it, it beat by roughly $7B on the top line and raised Q4 guidance by ~$5B over the Street — the Kress-led execution thesis is now a data point, not a hypothesis. That matters for anything downstream of GPU supply: the raise is almost entirely data center, Vera Rubin NVL72 is actually shipping (not slide-ware), and the Q4 guide bakes in zero China revenue, which means the $130B forecast has no dependency on the BIS remote-access rule from Nov 15 being unwound. For the broader compute-cost curve that every PyTorch, llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang workload rides on, this reads as: supply ramps faster, demand still outruns it, and the pricing floor underneath Blackwell/Rubin hardware stays firm into early 2027. Second, the board-decision thread. Harvey Jones's on-record statement that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang — made the same day a sitting president and the richest person alive publicly called for exactly that — is the clearest signal yet that this governance call was deliberate, not a reaction to the infidelity reporting. That removes the 'Huang could return in 60 days' branch from every downstream forecast. Third, the national-security layer: Huang and Teter appearing before congress on December 1–2 means the story is going to keep generating headlines through the first week of December, and the reported-Beijing-intelligence-asset angle is now in the public record alongside the export-controls thread from the BIS rule. The combination — a $115.8B print, a locked-in leadership transition, and a December congressional hearing — is the scaffolding that the GPT-6.2 Astra safety story, the California AG lawsuit, and the BIS remote-access rule will all get re-litigated around for the next three weeks. One thing didn't move: no permanent CEO has been named. That remains the open 30-day question. For Gabe's Python stack this is still far-field, but the practical takeaway is concrete: the AI compute market just told everyone it will not pause for a leadership transition, and the next governance signal worth watching is the shortlist — not whether the quarter would be good, which is now settled.

items.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon — mid-tier reasoning model with 1M context at $3/$15, retiring Gemini 3.1 Pro
items.summary: Google released Gemini 4 Neon on November 18, 2026, adding a mid-tier entry between Gemini 4 Hydrogen (high-end) and Gemini 4 Carbon/Argon (low-end) to its reasoning model family. The model supports up to 1,048,576 tokens (~1M) of context, accepts text, image, audio, video, and PDF inputs, and ships with four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and xhigh. Standard API pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens; cached-input is $0.15 per million. For comparison, Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon carry a launch-promo rate of $2/$10 through November 30 (rising to $4/$20 on December 1), making Neon the consistently-priced middle tier. Neon is available immediately via the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Android Studio, and in the Gemini app for AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers — it is not on the free tier. Google simultaneously announced the retirement of Gemini 3.1 Pro with this release, completing the transition to the Gemini 4 family.
items.why_it_matters: Google now has three distinct reasoning tiers in production: Hydrogen at the high end, Neon in the middle, and Carbon/Argon at the low end. The practical gap this fills is 1M context at a mid-tier price — $3/$15 sits noticeably below Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra while claiming competitive coding performance, and above Gemini 4 Carbon's post-promo $4/$20. The retirement of Gemini 3.1 Pro signals the full transition to the Gemini 4 family; there's no longer a 3.x model in the production lineup. The four thinking levels give callers meaningful cost control — running low-level thinking on routine tasks (summaries, code explanations) and xhigh on the genuinely hard ones (complex debugging, reasoning chains). For Gabe, the most concrete comparison point: any Python script or long HTML document he might want to pass to a model for review now has a 1M-context mid-tier option available in Google AI Studio today, without needing a Pro/Ultra subscription if accessed via the API. The enrichment run earlier this morning explicitly searched for Nov 18-19 Tier-1 model releases and came up empty — this was likely published early Nov 18 (US morning) before the enrichment window, and the DNS block on Google primary domains meant direct verification wasn't possible in that run either. Multiple independent secondary sources (shattered.io, computingforgeeks.com, cellcog.ai, aireleasetracker.com, kingy.ai, 9to5Google, VentureBeat) all report consistent specs.

items.title: Microsoft launches MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash at Ignite 2026 — in-house coding models at $0.50/M input (promo), claiming near-Opus coding quality in GitHub Copilot
items.summary: Microsoft unveiled MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash at Microsoft Ignite 2026 on November 17, as part of a slate of seven Microsoft AI (MAI) in-house models. MAI Code 2 targets enterprise coding tasks — multi-file debugging, repository-wide reasoning, and UI development — while Flash targets high-volume routine work such as code explanations, targeted edits, and rapid iterations. Microsoft claims MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's quality at 40% of the price and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's coding quality at 5% of the price, averaged across four internal benchmarks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas, FrontierCode v1.1) at a promotional rate. Independent community testing produced markedly lower scores; the Microsoft figures use controlled conditions and factor in the promo pricing. Promotional pricing: MAI Code 2 at $0.50 per million input tokens (rising to $1.00/M after May 17, 2027) and Flash at $0.05 per million input tokens (rising to $0.10). Both models are generally available in GitHub Copilot immediately; Flash is in limited preview in Microsoft Azure AI Foundry. Microsoft explicitly noted these models are not yet tuned for harder research problems or long-horizon agentic work.
items.why_it_matters: The price gap is the main claim worth noting: if Microsoft's benchmark numbers hold up, MAI Code 2 is offering Claude Opus 5.5-tier coding help at a 20x cost discount, delivered through GitHub Copilot, which a lot of developers already have open. The honest caveat is that Microsoft's internal benchmarks and community testing diverged significantly — Microsoft's figures use controlled conditions with the 50% promotional discount factored in. So treat the specific percentages as Microsoft's own positioning, not settled science. What is settled is the pricing: $0.50/M input is genuinely cheap for a model claiming frontier-adjacent coding quality, and Flash at $0.05/M is very cheap for routine tasks. The not-tuned-for-hard-research caveat matters: these are task-completion models designed for coding workflows, not reasoning-first architectures like Gemini 4 Neon or GPT-6.2 Astra. For Gabe: this doesn't directly affect his HTML/CSS/Python stack today, but if Copilot recommendations start feeling noticeably different in the next few weeks the MAI Code 2 swapover is the reason. The broader story is that Microsoft is now competing directly against OpenAI and Anthropic on the AI pricing curve — using the same Azure infrastructure that hosts the OpenAI partnership — which is a structural tension worth watching as the MAI family expands.
